chunks.text: BRAIn Lab EMNLP 2026 SimplexLoRA: Dynamic Rank Updating via Alternating Minimization with Simplex Projection Igor Shalygin 1,2,* , Grigorii Davydenko 1,2,3,* , Andrey Veprikov 1,2,3 , Aleksey Antonov 1,2,4 Nikolay Bushkov 4 , Stanislav Moiseev 4 , Aleksandr Beznosikov 1,2,5 1 Moscow Independent Research Institute of Artificial Intelligence (MIRAI) 2 Basic Research of Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (BRAIn Lab) 3 SB AI Lab 4 T-Technologies 5 Innopolis University * Equal contribution. The success of large language models in real-world applications relies on parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods such as Low-Rank Adaptation ( LoRA ), which inserts compact, trainable adapters into selected layers. In this paper, we propose SimplexLoRA , a LoRA variant that adaptively adjusts adapter ranks during fine-tuning based on their learned importance. Unlike standard LoRA , which employs a fixed rank across all layers, SimplexLoRA optimizes per-adapter importance weights on the n n -scaled simplex during a short warm-up and then freezes them, dynamically allocating capacity where it is most beneficial without increasing the overall parameter budget or inference cost. We evaluate SimplexLoRA across 12 language understanding, summarization, and reasoning tasks using DeBERTaV3, BART-large, Llama 3.1 8B, and Qwen3-8B. Our results show that SimplexLoRA consistently matches or outperforms standard LoRA and recent adaptive baselines, with the largest gains at low ranks. Our code is available at https://github.com/brain-lab-research/SimplexLoRA .

LoRA [ Hu et al., 2021 ] is a widely used parameter-efficient fine-tuning method [ Han et al., 2024 ] that parameterizes weight updates as 𝑾 ′ = 𝑾 0 + 𝑨 ​ 𝑩 {\bm{W}}^{\prime}={\bm{W}}^{0}+{\bm{A}}{\bm{B}} , with 𝑾 0 ∈ ℝ m × d {\bm{W}}^{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times d} frozen and trainable 𝑨 ∈ ℝ m × r , 𝑩 ∈ ℝ r × d {\bm{A}}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times r},{\bm{B}}\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times d} , r ≪ m , d r\ll m,d . This approach achieves low inference overhead and substantially reduces memory during fine-tuning. Figure 1: SimplexLoRA framework. Per-adapter importance weights are constrained to the n n -scaled simplex, enabling dynamic allocation of a fixed rank budget across layers. Despite its efficiency, standard LoRA uses a fixed rank across all layers, ignoring layer-wise differences in convergence and representation learning. Existing adaptive rank allocation methods attempt to address this issue but suffer from the critical drawbacks: (i) substantially more trainable parameters [ Sheng et al., 2025 ] , (ii) non-negligible inference-time overhead caused by dynamic pruning or gating mechanisms [ Zhang et al., 2025 ] , and (iii) deviations from the standard LoRA pipeline that hinder compatibility [ Zhang et al., 2023b ] . See Section 2 for further discussion. To address this limitation, we propose SimplexLoRA , which assigns an importance weight to each of the n n LoRA adapters, constrained to the n n -scaled simplex to enforce a fixed parameter budget. Key properties: (i) ranks learned automatically during fine-tuning; (ii) simplex constraint preserves the LoRA parameter budget; (iii) full LoRA compatibility; (iv) negligible training and inference overhead.

While LoRA has popularized parameter-efficient fine-tuning, it is not the only method to explore low-rank or structured adaptations. Earlier approaches include LoHA [ Nam et al., 2022 ] , which utilizes element-wise (Hadamard) interactions between low-rank matrices to reduce the parameter count without sacrificing expressivity, and Krona [ Edalati et al., 2022 ] , which employs the Kronecker product in place of the conventional low-rank matrix product to improve parameter efficiency while maintaining model capacity. Subsequent methods extended or refined the LoRA framework. VERA [ Kopiczko et al., 2023 ] reduces adapter storage by sharing frozen random projection matrices across layers and learning small scaling vectors. rsLoRA [ Kalajdzievski, 2023 ] replaces the original LoRA scaling factor α / r \alpha/r [ Hu et al., 2021 ] with the rank-stabilized factor α / r \alpha/\sqrt{r} . A complementary direction is taken by DoRA [ Liu et al., 2024 ] , which decomposes the adapted weight into magnitude and direction components and learns the magnitude together with a low-rank correction of the direction. Another line of work improves LoRA optimization and numerical efficiency. LoRA+ [ Hayou et al., 2024 ] uses different learning rates for the two adapter matrices, while QLoRA [ Dettmers et al., 2023 ] enables memory-efficient fine-tuning through 4-bit quantization of frozen base-model weights. Both are orthogonal to our adaptive rank allocation method and can be combined with it.

This topic is of particular relevance in the context of our work, as we focus on adaptive rank learning, enabling the model to automatically adjust the capacity of each adapter during fine-tuning. It has attracted significant attention in recent research [ Zhang et al., 2023a ; Zhang et al., 2023b ; Sheng et al., 2025 ] , as exploiting dynamically changing ranks allows models to utilize newly allocated parameters more efficiently. The SVD-like representation of LoRA adapters proposed in AdaLoRA [ Zhang et al., 2023b ] replaces the standard two-matrix adapter with the parameterization 𝑷 ​ Λ ​ 𝑸 {\bm{P}}\Lambda{\bm{Q}} and enables the construction of importance scores for individual singular components. Components outside the global importance budget are masked by setting the corresponding entries of Λ \Lambda to zero. To encourage the SVD-like structure, the method applies the orthogonality regularizer R ⁡ ( 𝑷 , 𝑸 ) = ‖ 𝑷 ⊤ ​ 𝑷 − 𝑰 ‖ F 2 + ‖ 𝑸 ⊤ ​ 𝑸 − 𝑰 ‖ F 2 . R({\bm{P}},{\bm{Q}})=\|{\bm{P}}^{\top}{\bm{P}}-{\bm{I}}\|_{F}^{2}+\|{\bm{Q}}^{\top}{\bm{Q}}-{\bm{I}}\|_{F}^{2}. During training, all three matrices 𝑷 {\bm{P}} , Λ \Lambda , and 𝑸 {\bm{Q}} are updated simultaneously. Although this parameterization avoids explicitly computing an SVD at every fine-tuning step, maintaining an initial rank above the target budget, regularly evaluating importance scores, and applying orthogonality regularization increase the training complexity compared with standard LoRA .

Several methods manage the rank budget more flexibly. ElaLoRA [ Chang et al., 2025 ] uses SVD-based adaptation and gradient-derived importance scores to prune and expand ranks at scheduled intervals. FlexLoRA [ Liu et al., 2026 ] uses normalized spectral entropy to guide rank pruning and expansion under a global budget. The dynamic-rank DoRA of Mao et al. [2024] decomposes adapters into structured rank-one components and prunes them based on per-component importance. NormAL LoRA [ Aastik et al., 2025 ] uses rank-norm regularization to determine an appropriate rank for each module. In a similar way, Sheng et al. [2025] proposes a rank-one LoRA series representation of the increment matrix: Δ ​ 𝑾 = 𝒃 1 ​ 𝒂 1 + … + 𝒃 p ​ 𝒂 p = [ 𝑩 p − 1 𝒃 p ] ​ [ 𝑨 p − 1 𝒂 p ] , \Delta{\bm{W}}={\bm{b}}_{1}{\bm{a}}_{1}+\ldots+{\bm{b}}_{p}{\bm{a}}_{p}=\begin{bmatrix}{\bm{B}}_{p-1}&{\bm{b}}_{p}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{\bm{A}}_{p-1}\\ {\bm{a}}_{p}\end{bmatrix}, where p p denotes the number of outer-loop iterations. This representation is applied to several layers, and after each outer-loop step a convergence criterion is evaluated: if the relative change between the ( p − 1 ) (p-1) -th and p p -th solutions is sufficiently small, the training of Δ ​ 𝑾 \Delta{\bm{W}} is terminated. Unlike IncreLoRA , which expands modules according to gradient-based importance scores, AROMA uses the relative Frobenius-norm change between consecutive solutions as a stopping criterion.

Compared with these works, SimplexLoRA does not force adapter ranks to strictly increase or rely on expensive SVD computations. Instead, we allow the ranks to be learned as continuous parameters, enabling the model to respond dynamically to the task’s complexity. By leveraging simplex projection and weight freezing, we obtain a direct form of rank adaptation that avoids explicit importance scoring and iterative pruning.

The weights ω = ( ω 1 , … , ω n ) \omega=(\omega_{1},\dots,\omega_{n}) are constrained to the n n -scaled simplex, where n n is the number of LoRA adapters. This preserves LoRA magnitude, with ω = ( 1 , … , 1 ) = 𝟏 \omega=(1,\dots,1)=\mathbf{1} recovering standard LoRA initialization [ Hu et al., 2021 ] . For T T steps, we perform standard LoRA fine-tuning by jointly optimizing the adapter parameters 𝒜 , ℬ \mathcal{A},\mathcal{B} and the importance weights ω \omega using gradient-based methods.

The weight vector ω \omega is projected onto the scaled simplex n ⋅ Δ n − 1 n\cdot\Delta_{n-1} via Euclidean projection [ Blondel et al., 2014 ] : min ω ^ ∈ n ⋅ Δ n − 1 ⁡ ‖ ω − ω ^ ‖ 2 2 . \min_{\hat{\omega}\in n\cdot\Delta_{n-1}}\|\omega-\hat{\omega}\|_{2}^{2}.

Adapter ranks are dynamically resized while preserving the total parameter budget: r i new = ⌊ r 0 ⋅ ω i ⌋ r_{i}^{\text{new}}=\lfloor r_{0}\cdot\omega_{i}\rfloor , where r 0 r_{0} is the initial (uniform) LoRA rank. When ranks change, the corresponding adapter matrices are resized and reinitialized following the standard LoRA scheme (see Appendix B ).

chunks.section: Phase 4. Standard LoRA training with new ranks.
chunks.text: After K K repetitions, we fix ω \omega to 𝟏 \mathbf{1} and reinitialize the adapter matrices 𝒜 \mathcal{A} and ℬ \mathcal{B} (Appendix B ). In this sense Phases 1–3 act as a short rank-search procedure: their role is to determine the per-layer rank allocation, while the warm-up adapter weights are intentionally discarded so that the final stage is functionally identical to standard LoRA with a non-uniform rank profile. Standard training then resumes with these fixed ranks, and any LoRA -based optimization algorithm can be applied. Figure 2: Scheduler for SimplexLoRA parameters.

To ensure that the model resumes training after freezing the weights, we employ a linear scheduler with two training phases (see Figure 2 ). The first phase includes rank training with reduced learning rate. Once rank training is complete, the learning rate is reset to zero, and the warm-up begins to train the resulting LoRA layers. Note, however, that the learning rate for ω \omega is fixed during training, the scheduler exclusively adjusts the LoRA weights. As a result, the subsequent fine-tuning phase is functionally identical to the standard LoRA training process.

The total number of rank updates, K ⋅ T K\cdot T , is kept small to avoid rank collapse and to ensure that the majority of training focuses on optimizing the LoRA adapters. In practice, T T is negligible compared to the overall training duration. In the ablation study (Section 4.3 ), we analyze the sensitivity of SimplexLoRA to both hyperparameters K K and T T , evaluating their impact on performance. Figure 3: Illustration of the rank distribution of SimplexLoRA . Figure 3 shows the final rank distribution from fine-tuning DeBERTaV3 base [ He et al., 2021 ] on the MRPC dataset from GLUE [ Wang et al., 2018 ] , tuning only self-attention layers. The learned distribution reveals a clear pattern: value projection matrices in self-attention layers consistently receive the highest ranks, indicating their critical role. Rather than eliminating ranks of adapters with low weights, the method reduces their magnitude, which helps mitigate underfitting.

We evaluate SimplexLoRA on a diverse set of benchmarks, including GLUE [ Wang et al., 2018 ] , XSum [ Narayan et al., 2018 ] , CNN/Daily Mail [ Chen et al., 2016 ] , GSM8K [ Cobbe et al., 2021 ] , BoolQ [ Clark et al., 2019 ] , and HellaSwag [ Zellers et al., 2019 ] . We exclude GLUE STS-B, whose regression metric requires custom evaluation and which overlaps with the QQP/MRPC similarity tasks. Experiments are conducted using DeBERTaV3 base [ He et al., 2021 ] , Llama 3.1 8B [ AI@Meta, 2024 ] , Qwen3-8B [ Yang et al., 2025 ] , and BART-large [ Lewis et al., 2020 ] models. Hardware and hyperparameters are provided in Appendix D .

We benchmark against baselines in default configurations under a number of training iterations. These span foundational PEFT methods (a performance floor) and recent dynamic-rank methods comparable to SimplexLoRA : Standard PEFT methods: LoRA [ Hu et al., 2021 ] , LoHA [ Nam et al., 2022 ] , Krona [ Edalati et al., 2022 ] , rsLoRA [ Kalajdzievski, 2023 ] , DoRA [ Liu et al., 2024 ] , and VERA [ Kopiczko et al., 2023 ] . Dynamic rank methods: AdaLoRA [ Zhang et al., 2023b ] , NormAL LoRA [ Aastik et al., 2025 ] , ElaLoRA [ Chang et al., 2025 ] , and FlexLoRA [ Liu et al., 2026 ] . In this setting (Table 1 ), where adapters are applied only to self-attention layers, full fine-tuning, standard LoRA , and SimplexLoRA emerge as the most robust methods, with SimplexLoRA achieving the best average score at the same 0.24 % 0.24\% parameter budget as standard LoRA . Other approaches require extensive hyperparameter tuning to achieve competitive performance. Consequently, we select standard LoRA as our primary baseline for further detailed comparison due to its widespread adoption and stability. Figure 4: The influence of hyperparameters on SimplexLoRA performance. As supplementary analysis, we grid-search hyperparameters on MNLI with DeBERTa to assess the robustness (Figure 4 ). Both methods are trained for 2048 steps using the best configuration from the main experiments; each cell reports the validation-accuracy difference. The results show that SimplexLoRA is stable under a limited optimization budget ( K ⋅ T < 100 K\cdot T<100 , i.e., less than 5% of total training). Very small values (e.g., K = 3 K=3 , T = 5 T=5 ) lead to underfitting due to insufficient rank adaptation, while larger values (e.g., K ≥ 10 K\geq 10 or T ≥ 15 T\geq 15 ) tend to cause rank overfitting. Beyond these thresholds, we find that increasing the number of projection steps and inner iterations results in a performance plateau, with values showing minimal deviation from the average. This confirms the importance of keeping K ⋅ T K\cdot T low to maintain efficiency without performance loss. In all experiments, we use K = 5 K=5 and T = 10 T=10 , which consistently yields strong performance.

We presented SimplexLoRA , a LoRA variant that allocates a fixed rank budget non-uniformly across layers via short alternating optimization on the n n -scaled simplex. Across 12 tasks and four backbones up to 8B parameters, SimplexLoRA matches or outperforms standard LoRA and recent adaptive baselines at the same parameter count and inference cost, with the largest gains in the low-rank regime.

The limitations of the proposed strategy are as follows. First, SimplexLoRA introduces three additional hyperparameters: the number of iterations between simplex projection steps T T , the total number of such projections K K , and the weight decay coefficient used for regularization; the ablation in Section 4.3 indicates that the method is robust within a broad range but does not eliminate the need to set these values. Second, the lack of experiments on models substantially larger than 8B parameters limits the generalizability of our findings. Third, while the per-task averages over three seeds consistently favor SimplexLoRA , on a few individual tasks (e.g., CoLA and RTE in the out-of-the-box DeBERTaV3 comparison) standard LoRA remains competitive or slightly better, indicating that the benefit of adaptive rank allocation is task-dependent. Fourth, a fundamental ambiguity remains during training: a small gradient norm in a layer may indicate either that the weights are well-optimized or that the gradients have vanished by the time they reach that layer, which can in principle bias the learned importance weights. On the ethical side, we see no specific risks beyond those already inherent to fine-tuning large language models: this work studies a parameter-efficient adaptation procedure, introduces no new data sources, uses only publicly available benchmarks with no proprietary or personal data and no human subjects, and reduces rather than increases the compute and memory footprint of fine-tuning.

SimplexLoRA uses this ranking as a proxy for layer importance and reallocates adapter rank accordingly: well-adapted layers receive higher ranks, weaker ones lower. We emphasize that this argument bounds the loss, not the rank distribution itself, so the connection to optimal ranks remains a heuristic; its empirical effectiveness is reported in Section 3 and the ablation in Section 4.3 . Note that to prevent ω \omega from degenerating into a one-hot vector, which is a common issue in simplex-constrained optimization where a single component dominates, one can apply regularization. In our implementation, we use a standard Euclidean regularization term to encourage ω \omega to remain closer to a uniform distribution across all components.

To ensure that the reinitialized adapters do not introduce immediate perturbations to the model’s output, we follow the standard LoRA initialization scheme. ∙ \bullet 𝑨 i {\bm{A}}^{i} initialized using the Kaiming uniform distribution [ He et al., 2015 ] to preserve the variance of activations: 𝑨 i ∼ U ⁡ ( − d i ​ n − 0.5 , d i ​ n − 0.5 ) , {\bm{A}}^{i}\sim U\left(-d_{in}^{-0.5},d_{in}^{-0.5}\right), ∙ \bullet 𝑩 i {\bm{B}}^{i} initialized to zero. While softmax and weighted softmax transformations are commonly used for projecting onto the simplex, we observed severe performance degradation during training when applying these methods. Their behavior is highly sensitive to temperature scaling: low temperatures tend to produce nearly one-hot distributions, whereas high temperatures result in almost uniform outputs. Such degeneracies are particularly problematic in our setting, where the goal is to efficiently allocate the rank budget across multiple adapters without inducing excessive sparsity or uniformity. For these reasons, we utilize the standard Euclidean regularization in the optimization problem formulation equation 1 , rather than alternatives such as KL divergence.
